hook_text: Vetkoek number seven hundred earns nothing at all — and it is the most important one of the month.
clip_script: A vetkoek stall at the taxi rank. Each vetkoek eats seven rand before it earns a cent — flour, oil, filling, gas, the paper packet. Those costs ride on every single one: make ten, spend seventy; make a hundred, spend seven hundred. But the stall spot and the gas bottle want three and a half thousand rand a month whether it rains all week or the queue never ends. Two kinds of cost: the ones that travel, and the ones that sit. She sells at twelve rand. So each vetkoek, after feeding itself, drops five rand into the tin toward that stubborn rent. Five rand — the contribution. How many five-rand payments cover three thousand five hundred? Seven hundred. Vetkoek number seven hundred is the break-even vetkoek: the moment the stall stops owing and starts earning. It makes no profit itself — it just opens the gate. From seven hundred and one onward, the full five rand is hers. She usually sells a thousand: three hundred past the line, times five — fifteen hundred rand of profit. Now watch what every examination watches: flour spikes, each vetkoek eats eight rand, contribution thins to four, and suddenly the rent needs eight hundred and seventy-five sales. She feels her break-even move the week prices move. That instinct — contribution against fixed costs — is the entire factory question, wearing an apron.
visual_style: A queue of glowing vetkoek marching toward a rent wall, each dropping a five-rand coin into a rising meter; the seven hundredth one lights the wall green; a flour price spike shrinks the coins to four rand and the wall stretches further away.
pacing: Quick sorting of the two cost kinds, steady coin-drop build to the green light, sharp jolt at the flour spike.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision session and carry break-even, budgets, reconciliations and VAT into your final exams in one sweep.
